<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Xiuying Wei
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>CLAIRE lab at EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:xiuying.wei@epfl.ch">xiuying.wei@epfl.ch</a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Caglar Gulcehre
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>CLAIRE lab at EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:caglar.gulcehre@epfl.ch">caglar.gulcehre@epfl.ch</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Structured dilated attention has an appealing inference-time efficiency knob: it reduces the FLOPs of the attention and the KV cache size by a factor of the dilation size <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, while preserving long-range connectivity. However, we find a persistent failure mode of them -sparsifying a pretrained attention model to a dilated pattern leads to severe accuracy degradation.
We introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RAT+</span>, a dense-pretraining architecture that augments attention with <em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">full-sequence recurrence</em> and <em id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">active recurrence learning</em>. A single RAT+ model is pretrained densely once, then flexibly switched at inference time to dilated attention (optionally with local windows) or hybrid layer/head compositions, requiring only a short 1B-token resolution adaptation rather than retraining separate sparse models. At 1.5B parameters trained on 100B tokens, RAT+ closely matches dense accuracy at <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=16}</annotation></semantics></math>  and drops by about 2-3 points at <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  on commonsense reasoning and LongBench tasks, respectively. Moreover, RAT+ outperforms attention when sparsifying to the top-k block attention. We further scale to 2.6B parameters and 200B tokens and observe the same trend.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Efficiency has become increasingly important for modern language models, as standard attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani, 2017</a>)</cite> incurs a quadratic cost in both FLOPs and memory with respect to sequence length. Among many orthogonal approaches to efficiency (e.g. low-bit representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jacob et al., 2018</a>)</cite> or faster optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jordan, 2023</a>)</cite>), a major line of work seeks to sparsify or replace the attention mechanism itself from the architectural perspective. Most of them can be grouped into two categories: training-from-scratch sparse architecture versus inference-time sparsification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The first design approach focuses on efficient architectures and trains them from scratch, including structured sparse attention (e.g., delicately designed dilated patterns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beltagy et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, local window attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohere et al., 2025</a>)</cite>), state space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu and Dao, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao and Gu, 2024</a>)</cite>, linear attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Katharopoulos et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and a recent RAT model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which inspired our architecture. Especially, RAT chunks the sequence, applies a forget-gate-like recurrence over attention keys and values within each chunk, and then performs inter-chunk attention (i.e., dilated attention) on the gated representations.
These models typically require retraining for each design configuration to achieve high efficiency and strong performance, which is costly and inflexible across downstream hardware and task requirements.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The second category focuses on inference-time sparsification, where a sparsified attention pattern is applied during inference. Dense pretrained models can often be sparsified into local <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> or importance-based patterns, such as top-k block attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, with different strengths. For example, local attention reduces both computational and memory footprints but can be limited in capturing long-range dependencies, whereas importance-based sparsification can better preserve accuracy but may introduce additional overhead.
Beyond these options, we find that dense attention fails to adapt to a classic structured pattern: <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">dilated attention</em>. Although dilated attention is hardware-friendly and can substantially reduce both FLOPs and KV cache usage while preserving long-range connectivity, sparsifying a dense model into a dilated pattern results in severe performance degradation, even when combined with local attention.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This raises a practical question: can we train a single model once and, at inference time, flexibly enable dilated attention and its hybrids without retraining separate sparse models? To address this, we study dilated attention from both perspectives: comparing it with RAT by training from scratch, and analyzing its sparsification from dense attention. Together, these results show that introducing a separate module, such as recurrence, is important for pretraining and necessary in the inference-time sparsification setting to explicitly construct a complete receptive field for dilated attention. Although RAT itself is a sparse architecture designed for training from scratch and cannot be directly used for sparse inference, we propose <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RAT+</span>, which retains a dense architecture during pretraining and enables flexible sparse inference. To ensure consistent recurrence behavior across different dilation settings, RAT+ adopts an overlapped chunk formulation, which further simplifies to full-sequence recurrence, and incorporates active recurrence learning. In brief, dilated attention requires an explicit mechanism to construct a complete receptive field; recurrence provides it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In experiments, we demonstrate that a pretrained RAT+ can be adapted to different dilated attention configurations (with optional local attention), as well as hybrid variants across layers and heads, using only 1B tokens for resolution adaptation. These variants maintain strong performance on short-context commonsense reasoning tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> (e.g., a dilation size of 16 brings 1-point accuracy drop, while allowing for 10× and 20× higher full-model maximum throughput for 1K-token decoding at context lengths of 4K and 16K, respectively), as well as on the LongBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2023</a>)</cite> benchmark. Moreover, we show that RAT+ performs better in top-k block pattern compared to the standard attention on needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) tasks in the RULER <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hsieh et al., 2024</a>)</cite> benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Instead of pretraining a sparse model, RAT+ is a dense architecture that enables more flexible inference-time efficiency.
Our main contributions include:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study the challenge of dilated attention in both training-from-scratch and inference-time sparsification settings. Based on these findings, we propose a novel dense architecture, RAT+, which incorporates full-sequence recurrence and active recurrence learning.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our proposed RAT+ architecture can be pretrained once and then adapted to different dilation sizes (with an optional local window) and hybrid variants, using only a 1B token for resolution adaptation. Moreover, we find that RAT+ outperforms attention-only models in top-k block attention.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We primarily pretrain models on the 1.5B scale on 100B tokens and evaluate different configurations on short-context, long-context, and retrieval-heavy tasks. Further experiments on larger scales, including 2.6B RAT+ models with 100B and 200B tokens, show that larger models exhibit a smaller loss gap between dense and dilated attention, demonstrating the scaling potential of RAT+.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We denote the sequence length with <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝚃</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, dilation size by <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, local window size by <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝚆</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, chunk size by <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙻</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the number of blocks selected in the attention of the top-k block by <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙺</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{K}</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D^{\dagger}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D^{\dagger}}</annotation></semantics></math> is used to highlight the attention model without recurrence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">We distinguish the size of the chunk from the dilation size below, noting that the original RAT sets <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L}=\mathtt{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝙳</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L}=\mathtt{D}</annotation></semantics></math>. Within each chunk, RAT first applies a simple linear recurrence over the attention keys <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒌</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{k}}</annotation></semantics></math> and values <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{v}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒗</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{v}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which reduces to forget-gate behavior with an input-dependent gate <math id="S2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{g}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒈</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{g}}</annotation></semantics></math>. For the token at position <math id="S2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E1X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\tilde{{\bm{v}}}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒗</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\tilde{{\bm{v}}}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle={\bm{g}}_{l}\odot\tilde{{\bm{v}}}_{l-1}+(1-{\bm{g}}_{l})\odot{\bm{v}}_{l}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒗</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mi>𝒗</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle={\bm{g}}_{l}\odot\tilde{{\bm{v}}}_{l-1}+(1-{\bm{g}}_{l})\odot{\bm{v}}_{l},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.E1Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\tilde{{\bm{k}}}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒌</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\tilde{{\bm{k}}}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle={\bm{g}}_{l}\odot\tilde{{\bm{k}}}_{l-1}+(1-{\bm{g}}_{l})\odot{\bm{k}}_{l}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒌</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mi>𝒌</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle={\bm{g}}_{l}\odot\tilde{{\bm{k}}}_{l-1}+(1-{\bm{g}}_{l})\odot{\bm{k}}_{l}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">It has <math id="S2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(1)</annotation></semantics></math> FLOPs and KV cache, and can be implemented through a one-step update in decoding and parallel scan in prefilling and training.
Then, for a token at position <math id="S2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> in dilation block <math id="S2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>, dilated attention is applied over the gated keys and values:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\bm{y}}_{b,d}=f([{\bm{q}}_{b,d}\tilde{{\bm{K}}}_{:,-1}^{\top};{\bm{q}}_{b,d}\tilde{{\bm{k}}}_{b,d}^{\top}])[\tilde{{\bm{V}}}_{:,-1};\tilde{{\bm{v}}}_{b,d}]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒚</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑲</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒌</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑽</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒗</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{y}}_{b,d}=f([{\bm{q}}_{b,d}\tilde{{\bm{K}}}_{:,-1}^{\top};{\bm{q}}_{b,d}\tilde{{\bm{k}}}_{b,d}^{\top}])[\tilde{{\bm{V}}}_{:,-1};\tilde{{\bm{v}}}_{b,d}],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p2.4" class="ltx_p">corresponding to the pattern shown in <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Inference-time sparsification ‣ 3 Motivation for recurrence ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 1</span></a>(c), which reduces both FLOPs and the KV cache size by a factor of <math id="S2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D}</annotation></semantics></math>. We do not consider the sliding variant, as it reduces parallelism during prefilling and training, and has to keep the full KV cache for decoding.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Motivation for recurrence</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze how the simple recurrence <a href="#S2.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq. (1)</span></a> enables effective dilated attention by bridging disconnected attention patterns. We study this from both the training-from-scratch and the inference-time sparsification perspectives.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training-from-scratch</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We find that the recurrence used in RAT plays a critical role in its subsequent inter-chunk attention (which corresponds to dilated attention), and we attribute this to its ability to provide a complete layer-wise receptive field.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To demonstrate this, we conducted experiments in <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Training-from-scratch ‣ 3 Motivation for recurrence ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a> comparing dilated attention with and without recurrence, as well as with optional local attention. We observe that dilated attention without recurrence fails to properly optimize and converges to suboptimal plateaus during training, as expected given the disconnected attention graph. While adding local attention links neighboring tokens to form a conceptually connected attention graph, it must also serve a distinct primary role: selectively aggregating fine-grained information within the local window for the current token. We hypothesize that this dual responsibility limits the ability of local attention to reliably support effective graph connectivity in dilated attention. In contrast, recurrence explicitly and independently provides such support. Moreover, even dense attention benefits from the introduction of recurrence, as shown in the last block of <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Training-from-scratch ‣ 3 Motivation for recurrence ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Results of training 1B-parameter models on 100B tokens from scratch, with or without the simple recurrence. All models are equipped with output gating (denoted as ogate below), which has been shown to be effective in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hua et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Perplexity (PPL) is measured on a held-out 0.5B-token validation set with a 4K sequence length, and Avg. CSR denotes the average across six commonsense reasoning tasks. Note that local attention typically achieves strong performance on short-context tasks while 7.96 at <math id="S3.T1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D^{\dagger}=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D^{\dagger}=64}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{W=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝚆</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{W=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  is a high PPL. See <a href="#A2.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 6</span></a> for implementation details and full results.</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Inference-time sparsification</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although dense attention models can be sparsified into local attention or importance-driven patterns such as top-k block attention, they do not adapt effectively to dilated attention, even when equipped with local attention, as shown in <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Inference-time sparsification ‣ 3 Motivation for recurrence ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 2</span></a>. We further apply a light degree of fine-tuning to assess whether this issue can be mitigated.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">First, lightly tuning a sparsified dilated attention pattern from a pretrained dense model yields a rapid loss decrease with a small number of tokens, after which the gains become much smaller, leaving a substantial gap relative to training from scratch. We view this initial rapid improvement as a <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">resolution-adaptation</em> process when switching from continuous dense attention to dilated connections. This effect is conceptually related to the fine-tuning used when adjusting positional encoding frequencies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">bloc97, 2023</a>)</cite>, but is simpler here, as it does not require attention length generalization. Moreover, because local attention in this setting is treated solely as an inference-time configuration and is not explicitly trained to construct a complete receptive field, there remains a clear performance gap relative to the training-from-scratch regime, potentially requiring prolonged, continued pretraining to close.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We tune the pretrained attention model with different numbers of tokens into the sparse variant (four initial tokens have already been added for attention sink <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>) and refer to the initial phase with rapid loss reduction (within a few hundred million tokens) as the resolution adaptation process. After this phase, improvements exist but much slower, as other modules such as local attention or the FFN are required to mitigate the performance gap, often requiring substantially longer retraining to match training-from-scratch (e.g., <math id="S3.T2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D^{\dagger}=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D^{\dagger}=64}</annotation></semantics></math>,<math id="S3.T2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{W=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝚆</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{W=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  as 7.96 and <math id="S3.T2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D^{\dagger}=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D^{\dagger}=1}</annotation></semantics></math>  as 7.44) performance. We also observe that hundreds of millions tokens is enough for RAT+ <a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ RAT+ adapting ‣ A.1 Implementation details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 7</span></a>, though we use 1B tokens in practice to ensure sufficient adaptation.
</span></figcaption>
<p id="S3.T2.5" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.T2.5.1" class="ltx_text">

</span></span></span></p>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In general, results from both aspects highlight the importance of explicitly constructing a complete receptive field for dilated attention, for example, via simple recurrence <a href="#S2.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq. (1)</span></a>. Although the efficient RAT architecture can address this problem in the pretraining setting, it does not extend directly to the inference-time sparsification regime. Next, we introduce an architecture designed to address this challenge.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18196v1/method.png" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/111;" width="452" height="111" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a) For architectural simplicity, we adopt an extreme overlapped setting, i.e., full-sequence recurrence with <math id="S3.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝚃</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=T}</annotation></semantics></math>. (b) Joint training to preserve dense attention capability while enforcing active recurrence learning with desired effective length <math id="S3.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L^{*}}=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L^{*}}=64</annotation></semantics></math>. (c) After pretraining, the resulting model can be efficiently adapted to various sparse inference patterns including effective results on dilated attention (optional local attention), and better performance on top-k block one compared to attention.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>RAT+: Dense model for sparse inference</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now propose a simple and novel architecture based on RAT for inference-time sparsification, where a single dense model is trained once (e.g. <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>) and effectively adapted at inference time to different sparse attention patterns, including dilated attention (e.g. <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1,2,4,8,16,32,64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>𝟸</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>𝟺</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>𝟾</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>𝟹𝟸</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1,2,4,8,16,32,64}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The RAT architecture is insufficient for this purpose, as it is a sparse design originally developed for training from scratch and obviously lacks the dense attention capability required in <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>. More concretely, the pretraining-free setting requires: (1) dense attention capacity together with a recurrence capacity that can reliably handle sequences of at least length 64 required in <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>; and (2) recurrence outputs follow the consistent distributions across different configurations, so that subsequent dilated attention does not have to cope with mismatched input distributions, which would otherwise hinder effective adaptation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Overlapped chunk size</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The RAT architecture sets the chunk size equal to the dilation size. For example, a recurrence trained with length <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  must be adapted to <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=4}</annotation></semantics></math>  when performing inference at <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=4}</annotation></semantics></math>. While it can handle shorter sequences, we observe that recurrence outputs at early time steps exhibit substantially different distributions (<a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 8</span></a>), making subsequent dilated attention difficult to adapt to this distribution shift. Such discrepancies at initial steps have also been identified as a form of covariate shift in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cooijmans et al., 2016</a>)</cite>. Consistently, the ablation results in the first row of <a href="#A2.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 7</span></a> show that adapting to small chunk sizes, which corresponds to initial time steps, leads to noticeably higher perplexity because of violating requirement (2).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Instead of applying normalization across time steps, which increases complexity and slows training, we use overlapped recurrence chunks with a fixed-length <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙻</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L}</annotation></semantics></math> for each token (i.e., each token is associated with a fixed-length recurrence window) throughout training and inference. During evaluation, the dilation size is varied while keeping <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙻</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L}</annotation></semantics></math> fixed (e.g., <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=64}</annotation></semantics></math>), satisfying the requirement (2) with the consistent recurrence outputs across different dilation settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Active recurrence learning</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also need to satisfy requirement (1) by learning both dense attention and recurrence abilities. However, in the current architecture, the overlapped recurrence is hierarchically applied to the attention key and value activations before the scaled dot-product operation. We find that directly training it leads to lazy recurrence learning. Because full-sequence attention already provides complete connectivity, the model can rely on it regardless of the effective range learned by the recurrence. As a result, the recurrence has little incentive to pursue the intended length capability and instead converges to a shorter length that is easier to learn. Empirically, we observe in <a href="#A2.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 7</span></a> that such models still exhibit high perplexity under sparse inference, though much better than attention.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To guarantee that the overlapped recurrence learns the required length (e.g., 64), we are motivated by the insight in <a href="#S3" title="3 Motivation for recurrence ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. 3</span></a> that a complete receptive field is critical for strong performance. We therefore introduce a stricter training configuration in which acquiring the desired recurrence capability provides a clear advantage over the shorter one. Concretely, we consider the sparse setting <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=64}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>, where insufficient recurrence capacity directly leads to degraded performance. Based on this, we adopt a simple joint training strategy that updates the model with a sparse case (<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=64}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>) and a dense case (<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=64}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>) per batch of data. The sparse case enforces active recurrence learning (ARL), while the dense case preserves sufficient attention capacity, ensuring strong performance in both dense and dilated settings. See <a href="#A2.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 7</span></a> for a comparison with another training strategy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Simplification</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, active recurrence learning allows us to further simplify the architecture by extending the overlapped chunk size <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{64}</annotation></semantics></math> to the sequence length without performance loss, resulting in a full-sequence recurrence in implementation. This change reduces training to a single parallel forward scan over the sequence and simplifies KV cache management for recurrence. The minimum required recurrence capability (e.g., 64) is then enforced by sparse dilated attention during joint training, while longer-length ability is learned only when favored by the training loss. Consequently, we denote the full-sequence recurrence by <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝚃</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=T}</annotation></semantics></math>  and use <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L^{*}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L^{*}}</annotation></semantics></math> for the actively enforced recurrence length when they differ. <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.3 Scaling up and down ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 6</span></a> and <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Design choices ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Subsec. 5.4</span></a> justify the choice of 64 based on the trade-off between the recurrence capacity and the flexibility of the dilation settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To conclude, as shown in <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Simplification ‣ 4 RAT+: Dense model for sparse inference ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 3</span></a>, with full-sequence
recurrence and active learning, RAT+ achieves dense performance comparable to attention while remaining effective in different dilation settings, with
even stronger sparse results than training RAT from scratch, benefiting from dense FLOPs training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
PPL performance of adapting different models to different dilation sizes with 1B tokens. Entries in the Train column marked with two settings denote training on both. For attention, we also include two variants trained under the same FLOPs with RAT+.
The failures of RAT at small dilation sizes come from its lack of dense-attention capability and the use of chunk sizes equal to the dilation size.
The gray row corresponds to the final RAT+ with full-sequence recurrence (<math id="S4.T3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝚃</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=T}</annotation></semantics></math>) and an active recurrence length of <math id="S4.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L^{*}=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L^{*}=64}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></figcaption>

<span id="S4.T3.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.10.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T3.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.10.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">7.66</span></span></span>
</span>
</span></span></span>
</span></span></span></p>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we first present the performance of RAT+ under various sparse inference patterns, including dilated, hybrid, and top-k block attention. We then report efficiency, scaling, and ablation studies.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Settings</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We primarily pretrain 1.5B-parameter models on 100B tokens from FineWeb-Edu <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Penedo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, using a context length of 4096. All models use output gating with a corresponding linear projection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hua et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>; RAT+ further includes one extra projection for the recurrence. We leave saving parameters for future work. Full implementation details are provided in the <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Implementation details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Subsec. A.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Unless otherwise specified (e.g., hybrid models), each sparse pattern is applied uniformly across all layers and used for both prefilling and decoding.</em> (1) In <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dilated attention with an optional local window</span>, we additionally add four initial tokens following StreamingLLM  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> for the attention sink problem in both accuracy and efficiency studies. This scheme reduces both FLOPs and KV cache size from <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(\mathtt{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝚃</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(\mathtt{T})</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(\mathtt{T}/\mathtt{D})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝚃</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>𝙳</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(\mathtt{T}/\mathtt{D})</annotation></semantics></math> with an optional <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(\mathtt{W})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝚆</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(\mathtt{W})</annotation></semantics></math>.
(2) In <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">hybrid design</span>, we evaluate the feasibility of hybrid layer-wise or head-wise sparse designs, rather than searching for optimal configurations which depend strongly on properties of the pretrained model (e.g., layer or head sparsifiability and preferred dilation). We leave the optimal choice for future work. (3)
<span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top-k block attention</span>
selects the most relevant blocks (block size indicated by dilation size <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, number <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙺</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{K}</annotation></semantics></math>) for each query token and computes attention only for them. We always choose the first and the most recent block, and leave the others to be decided by Quest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and MoBA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This scheme does not use adaptation and is applied directly. Note that it is less efficient than dilated or local attention (e.g., no KV cache reduction and extra block scoring).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of RAT+ on common-sense reasoning tasks.
Models in the first two blocks are obtained by adapting pretrained dense models with a lightweight adaptation stage of 1B tokens, while models in the third block are trained from scratch.
Task definitions and evaluation metrics follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and the results for the last two models are taken from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao and Gu, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
We report temporal-mixing FLOPs per token for each configuration.
All tasks involve short contexts with <math id="S5.T4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{T\leq 300}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝚃</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>𝟹𝟶𝟶</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{T\leq 300}</annotation></semantics></math>; in particular, LMB. and Wino. have even shorter contexts.
Thus large dilation settings almost reduce to a single recurrence.
The <math id="S5.T4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=128}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟸𝟾</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=128}</annotation></semantics></math>  is enabled via length generalization of the recurrence.</span></figcaption>
<div id="S5.T4.5" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:161.7pt;vertical-align:-78.9pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-47.4pt,22.2pt) scale(0.8,0.8) ;">

</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Main results</h3>

<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Does RAT+ preserve dense performance and enable stable dilation?</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Simplification ‣ 4 RAT+: Dense model for sparse inference ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 3</span></a>, RAT+ preserves perplexity for the dense pattern compared to attention-only models trained under the same FLOPs budget. Also, RAT+ remains stable across dilation settings, whereas attention-only models exhibit extremely high perplexity when directly sparsified into dilated attention (e.g., over 100 at <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We further evaluate the feasibility of dilated inference on downstream
commonsense reasoning benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for general language
understanding (<a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.1 Settings ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 4</span></a>). As shown in the table, <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=16}</annotation></semantics></math>  achieves nearly the same average accuracy as dense attention (<math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>), and <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  incurs only about a 2-point drop, while reducing temporal-mixing FLOPs by <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="64\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">LongBench performance of different sparse inference patterns. Due to space constraints, other less informative tasks are deferred to Appendix <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 9</span></a> (e.g., similar performance on LCC or uniformly low scores on MusiQue). Since LongBench is prompt-heavy where pretrained-only models can be sensitive to, we focus on overall trends. Moreover, for hybrid patterns, we present several representative examples to demonstrate feasibility rather than identifying optimal designs, as the optimal configuration depends on properties of the pretrained model (e.g., layer-wise sparsification preferences).
NQA: NarrativeQA; MF: MultiField-en; HQA: HotpotQA; 2WQA: 2WikiMultihopQA; RBP: RepoBench-P.
</span></figcaption>
