</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Does RAT+ support various sparse inference patterns?</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We then evaluate a wider range of efficient schemes on LongBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2023</a>)</cite> in <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Does RAT+ preserve dense performance and enable stable dilation? ‣ 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 5</span></a>, which consists of long-context tasks and is therefore suitable for studying sparse inference patterns. A key finding is that different downstream tasks favor different sparsification strategies, supporting our train-dense, adapt-sparse paradigm. For example, RBP task largely prefers the local attention pattern rather than the dilated one. By combining them within each layer or in different layers can recover the performance back to 26. Also, inserting a small number of dense layers can benefit tasks such as MF.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For hybrid sparse inference patterns, we emphasize that our goal is to demonstrate the feasibility, rather than to identify optimal hybrid designs. For example, the hybrid configuration of <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=16}</annotation></semantics></math>  interleaved with <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{W=1024}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝚆</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟶𝟸𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{W=1024}</annotation></semantics></math>  achieves intermediate performance, with clear improvements over local-window-only models (e.g., +4 points on 2WQA), but does not outperform the dilated one on average. This is because, <em id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">unlike training-from-scratch regime where functionality can be freely allocated across modules during optimization, inference-time hybrid configurations are constrained by the pretrained specialization of layers and heads.</em> Different components may vary in how amenable they are to sparsification, as well as in the dilation or window sizes at which they operate most effectively. We leave the search of optimal hybrid sparse patterns to future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">More results include length generalization with the NTK-based RoPE scaling method <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">bloc97, 2023</a>)</cite>, which allows us to either increase FLOPs proportionally or keep them unchanged by expanding the dilation size when extending to longer sequence lengths, as well as additional NIAH results in Appendix <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 10</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18196v1/niah.svg" id="S5.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/251;" width="476" height="251"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S5.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Results of top-k block attention with block size <math id="S5.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D}</annotation></semantics></math> and number of selected blocks <math id="S5.F2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙺</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{K}</annotation></semantics></math> on the hard NIAH-MK-2 and NIAH-MK-3 tasks from the RULER benchmark with <math id="S5.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{T=4096}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝚃</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟺𝟶𝟿𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{T=4096}</annotation></semantics></math>. RAT+ (no ARL in SFT) means disabling active recurrence learning during the SFT, which further demonstrates the benefit of the recurrence. More results include remaining tasks in <a href="#A3.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 11</span></a>, MoBA-style top-k block attention in <a href="#A3.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 12</span></a>, dilated attention in <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 10</span></a></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18196v1/eff.svg" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/299;" width="476" height="299"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F3.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S5.F3.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Efficiency results of the temporal-mixing operator on a single GH200 GPU, covering both prefilling and decoding scenarios with hidden dimension <math id="S5.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙷</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{H}</annotation></semantics></math>. Prefilling latency is measured on sequences of 262K tokens.
Decoding latency is measured for 256 or 128 batches of tokens for the two hidden dimensions, respectively; the baseline runs out of memory beyond 32K tokens.
We use <span id="S5.F3.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">FlexAttention</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for prefilling (with <math id="S5.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>  reducing to FlashAttention), and <span id="S5.F3.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">FlashAttention</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>for decoding. Recurrence is implemented by <span id="S5.F3.7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">associative scan</span> in PyTorch for prefilling and a simple step update for decoding.
Due to space constraints, additional results are reported in <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix D</span></a>.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18196v1/thr.svg" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/149;" width="476" height="149"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Maximum decoding throughput (tokens/sec) of the full 1.5B and 7B models for decoding
1024 tokens, measured at context lengths of 4096 and 16384, corresponding to
prefilling lengths of 3072 and 15360 tokens, respectively.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Does recurrence help beyond dilation (top-k block)?</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond dilated attention, we also evaluate performance when directly sparsified to top-k block attention in <a href="#S5.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Does RAT+ support various sparse inference patterns? ‣ 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 2</span></a>, <a href="#A3.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 11</span></a> and <a href="#A3.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 12</span></a>. Interestingly, we find that top-k block attention performs substantially better when sparsified from RAT+ than from attention-only models. We hypothesize that recurrence encourages token representations to better reflect the content of their block, so that block selection algorithms (e.g., min/max or mean pooling) can capture this information more effectively. This in turn leads to more accurate block scoring and improves final performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use the NIAH tasks from the RULER benchmark to illustrate this effect. These retrieval-heavy tasks are particularly sensitive to block selection quality. To exclude prompt sensitivity in pretrained-only models, we apply a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage to make models faithfully follow instructions before all evaluations. In <a href="#S5.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Does RAT+ support various sparse inference patterns? ‣ 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 2</span></a>, all dense configurations achieve perfect accuracy, whereas sparse variants from attention-only models suffer significant degradation. Compared to them, sparse variants from RAT+ maintain much higher accuracy (e.g., 93.8 vs. 63.2 on NIAH-MK-2 at <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{K=16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙺</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{K=16}</annotation></semantics></math>). Moreover, enabling active recurrence learning during SFT by jointly tuning the dense and corresponding dilated variants is critical, as it allows recurrence to actively absorb task-specific information. Consistent improvements across other NIAH tasks and an additional top-k block attention method are reported in the <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix C</span></a>. We also present an interesting finding there when comparing these results with those of dilated attention.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">What are the actual latency/throughput wins?</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">First, for prefilling latency, linear projections dominate at short sequence lengths, while the temporal-mixing operator for attention becomes the main bottleneck at longer contexts. At 4K length, full-sequence recurrence incurs latency comparable to well-optimized FlashAttention, but this overhead becomes relatively minor once linear projections are included (<a href="#A4.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 14</span></a>) or when sequence lengths further increase. At long sequence lengths, the RAT+ operator with <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=16}</annotation></semantics></math>  achieves up to <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="6.3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>6.3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.3\times</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="8.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedups for hidden dimensions 2048 and 4096 at 262K prefilling length, respectively. When benchmarking the temporal-mixing block with linear layers included, where the extra recurrence projection and shared projection overhead reduce the measured speedup, we still obtain <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="6\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6\times</annotation></semantics></math> improvements over the attention block, as shown in <a href="#A4.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 14</span></a> and <a href="#A4.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 16</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For decoding latency (see <a href="#A4.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 15</span></a> and
<a href="#A4.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 17</span></a>), temporal-mixing operator dominates even when
generating tokens at moderate positions such as 4K. We found that when GPU resources are
sufficiently utilized (e.g., larger batch sizes, hidden dimensions, or longer sequence), RAT+ can yield wall-clock speedups close to the dilation
factor (e.g., <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="14\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14\times</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=16}</annotation></semantics></math>) at the operator level. In this regime, linear projections with the extra one contribute relatively little to decoding latency, so the block-level speedups closely match those observed at the operator level.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, in <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Does RAT+ support various sparse inference patterns? ‣ 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 4</span></a>, we benchmark end-to-end throughput on full models with 1.5B and 7B
parameters, where jointly reducing KV cache size
and FLOPs, <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  can achieve over <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="60\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60\times</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="40\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40\times</annotation></semantics></math> better throughput respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Scaling up and down</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also perform scaling experiments to demonstrate that the proposed RAT+ architecture generalizes across different model sizes and datasets. For the smaller scale, we train a 200M-parameter model on the PG19 book dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rae et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, with detailed results reported in the <a href="#A2.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 8</span></a>. For the larger scale, we scale the 1.5B model up to 2.6B parameters and optionally consider training with more tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.3 Scaling up and down ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 5</span></a>, the loss gap between <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  and <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>  becomes noticeably smaller at the 2.6B scale (downstream evaluations are provided in the <a href="#A3.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 13</span></a>). We attribute this to the increased capacity of recurrence with a larger hidden dimension, which better supports modeling 64 length.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18196v1/2x6b.svg" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/292;" width="452" height="292"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Scaling-up experiments.
We report validation loss on a held-out 0.5B-token subset of the FineWeb dataset to illustrate the loss gap between dense and sparse configurations. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18196v1/chunk_size.svg" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/283;" width="429" height="283"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Choice of <math id="S5.F6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=64}</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S5.F6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L^{*}=16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L^{*}=16}</annotation></semantics></math> means <math id="S5.F6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>  and <math id="S5.F6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=16}</annotation></semantics></math>  joint training to enable 16 length capability for recurrence. Different performance on <math id="S5.F6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>  comes from different training FLOPs and different recurrence abilities in capturing the corresponding length. Grey points indicate recurrence length generalization.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Design choices</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned in <a href="#S4" title="4 RAT+: Dense model for sparse inference ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. 4</span></a>, the ablation studies for the two techniques are reported in <a href="#A2.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 7</span></a>. Here, we briefly discuss other design choices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Why recurrence?</span> We adopt recurrence primarily for its simplicity compared to MLPs, convolutions, attention, and linear attention. In contrast, these alternatives are heavier and more complex, which may introduce optimization difficulties in this hierarchical architecture. A second motivation is input-dependent temporal modeling. The recurrence employed here uses input-conditioned forget gates, which adapt to the dynamics of text sequences. MLPs are not time-variant, and both convolutions and attention require interactions with all tokens within the chunk, and thus would require more parameters under the overlapped chunk size.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">How recurrence?</span> Our design follows RAT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which applies recurrence to attention keys and values in a hierarchical manner. Similar designs have also appeared in recent work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, using different modules and targeting different objectives. We evaluate other variants in Appendix <a href="#A2.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 8</span></a>, and the adopted design consistently performs best.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Choice of <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=64}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span>
This is an empirical choice in RAT+. Intuitively, <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  is not a large sequence length, and recurrence can handle it reliably without suffering from memory degradation in long-context modeling. At the same time, it is not a small value: by covering dilation up to 64, it provides sufficient flexibility for choosing dilation sizes and constructing hybrid models with high speed-up. Moreover, it is safer for length generalization compared to <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=16}</annotation></semantics></math>. We also ablate other active recurrence lengths, as shown in <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.3 Scaling up and down ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 6</span></a>. Taking these trade-offs and empirical results into account, we finally choose <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  in this paper.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Related works</h2>

<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Efficient pretrained architectures</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Many efficient architectures are designed and trained from scratch as alternatives to dense attention, including structured sparse patterns such as sliding-window and dilated attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beltagy et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zaheer et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hassani and Shi, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohere et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Dilated-only schemes often require careful rate compositions to ensure full receptive fields and can be harder to optimize than dense models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fournier et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hamaguchi et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. Other recent approaches build on state space models and linear attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu and Dao, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao and Gu, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Katharopoulos et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orvieto et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, exploring the duality between linear recurrence and linear attention. A closely related architecture is RAT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which hierarchically combines recurrence and attention and can interpolate between them. Our analysis builds upon RAT, motivated by the observation that its inter-chunk attention mechanism is indeed dilated attention and yields strong training performance with recurrence. Finally, a key limitation of such efficient pretrained architectures is that
they typically require training from scratch for each configuration (e.g.,
dilation size in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beltagy et al., 2020</a>)</cite> or chunk size in RAT), which largely
reduces inference-time flexibility across different task preferences and
efficiency budgets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Sparse inference for attention models</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Many works also study inference-time sparsification of standard attention, motivated by the sparsity of attention maps. One direction emphasizes local attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and its hybrids <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, while another identifies important tokens or blocks for each query token. Such importance-driven methods have been explored for both prefilling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and decoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oren et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025)</a></cite> additionally applies continued pretraining to train a dedicated indexer. While sparsifying dense attention into these patterns is often effective, we explore the case of dilated attention, which dense pretrained models fail severely. We highlight it as an important structured pattern for its long-range
connections beyond local-window schemes and its clean reductions in both FLOPs
and KV cache size compared to most importance-driven approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion and Future work</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">RAT+ points to a promising direction for efficiency: designing dense
architectures that retain full dense capability while supporting a broader set of
sparse inference patterns, rather than training separate sparse
architectures from scratch. Large-scale experiments demonstrate the
effectiveness of full-sequence recurrence and active recurrence learning for
supporting dilated inference, highlighting RAT+’s potential for future language
model development.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Future work</span> Although we have demonstrated substantial speedups, the
efficiency of RAT+ could further benefit from dedicated CUDA-level
optimizations. From the pretraining perspective, our approach may be extended
to other domains and larger scale, and potentially applied to tokenizer-free settings with byte-level inputs. From the inference perspective, identifying
optimal hybrid sparse configurations is also an interesting direction for
future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Appendix</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Implementation details</h3>

<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implementation for <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Training-from-scratch ‣ 3 Motivation for recurrence ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a>.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We largely follow the RAT implementation, using the same model architecture and training dataset but also some modifications. RAT shares linear projections for attention queries and keys across heads to match the parameter count of standard attention. In our implementation, we do not take this parameter sharing; instead, we keep dense linear projection for the recurrence and leave further lightweight considerations for future work. For the results in the third block, we simply adopt full-sequence recurrence and find that it improves performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">RAT+ pretraining</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the 1.5B-parameter model, we use a model dimension of 2048, 24 Transformer layers, and a head dimension of 128, equipped with RMSNorm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and Sennrich, 2019</a>)</cite> and no bias terms. The context window is set to 4096. We use standard RoPE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al., 2024</a>)</cite> instead of the inter-chunk RoPE used in RAT, for easier management of positional encoding, and put it after the recurrence function. The RoPE based is set to 10,000. Model parameters are initialized from a Gaussian distribution with a standard deviation of 0.02. We adopt the LLaMA2 tokenizer in all experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The optimization hyperparameters follow the rule described in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bi et al. (2024)</a></cite>. We use a cosine-annealed learning rate schedule with a peak learning rate of <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8.0\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8.0\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, decaying to <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math>, and 5% warmup. The global batch size is set to 512.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For the 2.6B-parameter model trained on 100B tokens, we increase the model dimension to 2560 with 28 layers. All other hyperparameters are kept the same, except that we use a peak learning rate of <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7.0\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>7.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.0\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> and a global batch size of 640. For the 200B-token training setting, the peak learning rate remains <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7.0\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>7.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.0\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> with a global batch size of 768, following the same rule in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bi et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">RAT+ adapting</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The adaptation process uses 1B randomly sampled tokens from the FineWeb-Edu dataset. We use the original batch size and a small learning rate, e.g., 2.0e-5. In practice, we find that the training loss during adaptation stabilizes within a few hundred million tokens, as shown in Figure <a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ RAT+ adapting ‣ A.1 Implementation details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 7</span></a>. To ensure sufficient adaptation, we use 1B tokens in all experiments.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18196v1/adapt_final.svg" id="A1.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/179;" width="429" height="179"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A1.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Validation loss curves for adapting different models with 1B tokens. It is evident that models with various dilated patterns quickly adjust and achieve stable loss values within a few hundred million tokens. We employed a simple optimization scheme with no warmup, which may explain the slight loss increase of <math id="A1.F7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>  at the beginning, after which it recovers.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation setup largely follows the settings used in RAT, except for the NIAH tasks. We construct a dataset of approximately 7M tokens and apply a single-stage SFT before all evaluations. Compared to RAT, we sweep SFT for four epochs instead of one, to ensure that all models faithfully follow instructions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficiency</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The decoding implementation is straightforward, requiring only a single update for the recurrence and the use of the <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">SDPA</span> kernel in PyTorch. For training and prefilling, the recurrence is implemented using the <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">associative scan</span> in PyTorch. In the attention computation, we first use <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">flex attention</span> to handle the dilated connections by applying a dilation-level mask and returning the softmax denominator. We then compute the local and initial connections. The online softmax technique <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Milakov and Gimelshein, 2018</a>)</cite> is used to gather the results from the two parts. We expect that the efficiency of RAT+ can be further improved with dedicated CUDA kernel-level optimizations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Supporting materials for Method</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we include detailed evaluation results on commonsense reasoning tasks for <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Training-from-scratch ‣ 3 Motivation for recurrence ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a> in <a href="#A2.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 6</span></a>, visualizations of the different distributions at the initial recurrence steps in <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 8</span></a>, ablation studies for the proposed method in <a href="#A2.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 7</span></a>, and perplexity results on PG19 in
<a href="#A2.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix B Supporting materials for Method ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 8</span></a>.</p>
</div>

</figure>
<figure id="A2.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18196v1/recurrence_distribution.svg" id="A2.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/167;" width="476" height="167"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A2.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">L2 norm values of recurrence outputs at different time steps.
We observe that the outputs at early time steps differ significantly. The first row shows an initialized network using our simple recurrence at layers 0, 6, 18, and 23. The second row corresponds to the same initialized network but with a non-zero initial cell state provided to the recurrence. The third row shows the results of the pretrained network. We visualize the outputs of our simple recurrence here; a similar phenomenon has also been observed in standard recurrent networks, as reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cooijmans et al. (2016)</a></cite>.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A2.T7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 7</span>: </span><span id="A2.T7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ablation studies of RAT+. All configurations are adapted from the corresponding pretrained models with 1B tokens, except for the w/o adaptation case. In the RAT+ ablation block: (1). the first row sets <math id="A2.T7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙻</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L}</annotation></semantics></math> equal to <math id="A2.T7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D}</annotation></semantics></math> at inference, and thus suffers from distribution shifts at the initial recurrence steps, leading to poor performance at <math id="A2.T7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=1}</annotation></semantics></math>; (2). The second row performs worse than RAT+ because dense connectivity is not sufficiently learned; (3). The third row removes active recurrence learning. although dense performance is preserved, recurrence is not learned effectively, resulting in degraded performance at larger dilation sizes due to an incomplete receptive field; (4). The fourth row shows results without adaptation for our final variant. Note that even <math id="A2.T7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=64}</annotation></semantics></math>  still requires adaptation, since four initial tokens are additionally added at inference.
</span></figcaption>

<figure id="A2.T8" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A2.T8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 8</span>: </span><span id="A2.T8.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
PPL performance of a 200M RAT+ model on the PG19 book dataset with a context length of 8192. The first row shows strong performance across dilation settings. The second and third rows report additional design-choice ablations. As can be seen, removing recurrence over the attention keys leads to a slight increase in perplexity. We think this might because the gated representations on the attention values can still be propagated across layers. In contrast, applying recurrence to the input of the <span id="A2.T8.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">qkv</span> projections results in clear worse performance, with <math id="A2.T8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=4}</annotation></semantics></math>  even higher than the <math id="A2.T8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=128}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟸𝟾</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=128}</annotation></semantics></math>  setting of the standard RAT+ variant.</span></figcaption>

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Additional downstream evaluation results</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we provide additional downstream evaluation results on the remaining LongBench tasks in <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 9</span></a>, on NIAH tasks in <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 10</span></a>, <a href="#A3.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 11</span></a> and <a href="#A3.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 12</span></a>, and evaluation results of 2.6B model in <a href="#A3.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix C Additional downstream evaluation results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 13</span></a>. We observe an interesting difference between dilated attention and top-k block
attention on the NIAH tasks. Dilated attention appears to find NIAH-S-3 more challenging than NIAH-MK-2, NIAH-MQ, and NIAH-MV, with worse performance on NIAH-S-3. In contrast, top-k block attention treats NIAH-S-3 as an easier task relative to these three. We think this reflects the interaction between task characteristics and
sparsification patterns. NIAH-S-3 and NIAH-MK-3 involve retrieving 32-digit UUID strings, where dilated attention with large dilation sizes may fail to capture the exact sequence; even a single incorrect digit leads to a complete loss of score. On the other hand, MQ, MV, and MK tasks involve multiple keys, queries, and values, which place a heavier burden on top-k block attention to identify the critical blocks, especially under less favorable configurations of <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝙺</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{K}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T9" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T9.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 9</span>: </span><span id="A3.T9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Supplementary results on additional LongBench tasks. We omit these results from the main text as they are less representative.
All models perform poorly on MusiQue and exhibit very similar performance on LCC. For the remaining summarization tasks, we observe that pretrained-only models tend to repeat prompts or outputs, which makes the quantitative results less reliable. But it can be seen that our dilated attention maintains performance close to the dense baseline with
the gap generally increases as the dilation size becomes larger.
</span></figcaption>
<div id="A3.T9.5" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:155.4pt;vertical-align:-75.4pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-15.7pt,7.1pt) scale(0.9,0.9) ;">
<p id="A3.T9.5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T9.5.1.1" class="ltx_text">
<span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:376.4pt;height:169.6pt;vertical-align:-82.3pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(0.0pt,0.0pt) scale(1,1) ;">
<span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text">
<span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<span class="ltx_tbody">
<span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RAT+</span> (<math id="A3.T9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L^{*}=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L^{*}=64}</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>
<span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Musique</span></span>

<span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">QMSUM</span></span>
<span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T9.5.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MultiNews</span></span>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 10</span>: </span><span id="A3.T10.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Retrieval ability<span id="A3.T10.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">: Accuracy performance with exact match scoring on the Needle-in-Haystack tasks with different configurations from the RULER benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hsieh et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We use <math id="A3.T10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{T=4096}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝚃</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟺𝟶𝟿𝟼</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{T=4096}</annotation></semantics></math> and bold less favorable results. We found they mainly occur when the text query/key/values are the UUID, and may wrongly copied part of the answers. Also, in NIAH-MK-2, bigger dilation size also performs worse.</span></span></figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T12.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 12</span>: </span><span id="A3.T12.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Retrieval ability of the top-k block attention for different models. On the following three pretrained plus SFT models, we apply MoBA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> style top-k block attention, where the critical block is determined by the mean pooling of attention keys within each block. We found that this style performs worse than the Quest in the training-free manner, but RAT+ still outperforms the baseline a lot.</span></figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T13.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 13</span>: </span><span id="A3.T13.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of 2.6B RAT+ on common-sense reasoning tasks (<math id="A3.T13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{T\leq 300}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝚃</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>𝟹𝟶𝟶</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{T\leq 300}</annotation></semantics></math>) pretrained on 100B and 200B tokens, respectively. We use <math id="A3.T13.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{L^{*}=64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝙻</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟼𝟺</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{L^{*}=64}</annotation></semantics></math> and enable the <math id="A3.T13.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{D=128}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝙳</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟷𝟸𝟾</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{D=128}</annotation></semantics></math>  setting via length generalization of the recurrence.</span></figcaption>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Additional efficiency results</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we provide detailed and more efficiency results in <a href="#A4.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 14</span></a>, <a href="#A4.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 15</span></a>, <a href="#A4.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 17</span></a>, and <a href="#A4.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Appendix D Additional efficiency results ‣ RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 17</span></a>. We also mark out some speed-ups in the tables.</p>

  <div class="keyboard-glossary">
    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
